tip: When a preposition meets an indefinite article, contraction is optional in some cases: 'dum/duma' exist but 'de um/de uma' is also fine.
'Se fala' – impersonal construction with 'se', expressing a general statement about what 'one does' or 'is done'.

target: A gente gosta de fazer trilha.
tip: 'Fazer trilha' means to hike. Brazilians use 'fazer' in many leisure expressions: fazer mergulho (dive), fazer escalada (climb), fazer rapel (rappel).
Different from Spanish `gustar` (which flips the subject). Portuguese `gostar` works straightforwardly: subject + gostar + de + thing.
Adjectives agree in gender: 'deliciosa' (fem.) matches 'comida' (fem.). Masculine would be 'delicioso.'
The preposition 'por' contracts with articles: por+o=pelo, por+a=pela – meaning 'through the' or 'by the'.

target: Ela é bem humorada e divertida.
tip: The 'a' preposition contracts with 'a' article to form 'à' – the grave accent marks this crasis: 'Vou à escola'.

target: Eu tô precisando de um café.
tip: 'precisando' – gerund form for ongoing action. Brazilian Portuguese prefers 'estar + gerund' over European Portuguese's 'estar a + infinitive'.
Sertanejo is Brazil's most popular music genre – a country-style music with modern pop influences. It's everywhere in Brazil.
'Gostar de' always requires the preposition 'de.' You can't say 'gosto praia' – it must be 'gosto de praia.'
Contractions happen automatically in speech but must be written correctly: 'no parque' not 'em o parque'.
Plural contractions follow the same pattern: de+os=dos, em+as=nas, a+os=aos – the rule applies to all number/gender combos.
'Ainda bem que' means 'thank goodness that' or 'it's a good thing that.' Expresses relief.

target: Ela gosta muito do trabalho dela.
tip: When 'gostar de' is followed by a definite article, contractions happen: gostar do (de + o), gostar da (de + a), gostar dos/das.

target: A minha avó é muito carinhosa.
tip: 'Carinhosa' – feminine -osa ending to match 'avó' (grandmother). Masculine: 'carinhoso.'

target: Ela é loira de olhos azuis.
tip: 'De olhos azuis' is how you describe eye color in Portuguese – literally 'of blue eyes.' Same pattern for hair: de cabelos pretos.

target: Com licença, onde fica o banheiro?
tip: 'Com licença' is used when you need to get past someone or interrupt politely. It's more common than 'desculpe' for these situations.

english: See you tomorrow, get some rest!
tip: The perfeito often pairs with time markers: 'ontem' (yesterday), 'na semana passada' (last week), 'em 2020'.

english: Have a good trip! Send news.
tip: Don't confuse perfeito with the present perfect – Portuguese 'tenho feito' implies ongoing/recent action, not a completed one.

english: We prefer to go by car.
tip: 'Preferir' = to prefer. Unlike 'gostar' and 'precisar,' it does not take 'de': 'preferimos ir' (not 'de ir').

english: How annoying, I missed the bus!
tip: The perfeito tells the story – it moves the narrative forward with completed events, one after another.

english: Did you make a hotel reservation?
tip: Portuguese has two `you`s: `tu` (informal, PT/southern BR) and `você` (universal in BR). Different verb forms: `tu falas` vs `você fala`.

target: Pois não? Em que posso ajudar?
english: Of course? How can I help you?
tip: 'Pois não' is a formal/polite way to say 'how can I help you.' You'll hear it from shopkeepers, receptionists, and servers.

target: A gente gosta de viajar no Carnaval.
english: We like to travel during Carnival.
tip: 'A gente gosta de' – remember 'a gente' takes singular: 'gosta' not 'gostamos.' 'No Carnaval' = during Carnival.

target: Ela gosta de ler antes de dormir.
english: She likes to read before bed.
tip: 'Gostar de' + infinitive: 'gosta de ler.' 'Antes de' = before. 'Antes de dormir' = before sleeping.

target: Os filhos dela são educados e obedientes.
english: Her children are polite and obedient.
tip: 'Educados e obedientes' – plural adjectives agree with plural noun 'filhos.' 'Dela' = de + ela = her.

target: A minha cachorra é pequena e branca.
english: My dog is small and white.
tip: Colors agree with gender and number: branco/branca/brancos/brancas. Some colors don't change: laranja, rosa, violeta.

target: Eu vi ela no supermercado ontem.
english: I saw her at the supermarket yesterday.
tip: 'Ver' past: eu vi. 'Vi ela' is informal; formal would be 'a vi.' But 'vi ela' is standard in speech.

target: A gente pôde sair mais cedo ontem.
english: We were able to leave early yesterday.
tip: 'Poder' in the past: pude, pôde, pudemos, puderam. Note the circumflex on 'pôde' (past) to distinguish from 'pode' (present).

english: I'll be right back, wait just a minute.
tip: The diminutive '-inho' softens requests. 'Um minutinho' (a little minute) sounds much more polite than 'um minuto.'

target: Nada a ver, não foi isso que eu disse.
english: That has nothing to do with it; that's not what I said.
tip: 'Nada a ver' means 'nothing to do with it' or 'that's not it.' A very common expression for disagreement.

target: Eu quis te ligar, mas era muito tarde.
english: I wanted to call you, but it was too late.
tip: 'Querer' past: eu quis. 'Quis te ligar' = wanted to call you. 'Era muito tarde' = it was too late.
'Valeu' is the most casual way to say 'thanks' in Brazil. It literally comes from 'valer' (to be worth). Very informal but used everywhere.
'Nenhum/nenhuma' (none/not any) – stronger than simple 'não', emphasizing complete absence.
For repeated past actions with a set number, use perfeito: 'Li o livro três vezes' (I read the book three times).
'Viu' (literally 'did you see') is added at the end of sentences as a tag question meaning 'okay?' or 'got it?'. Very Brazilian.
'Tá bom' is the casual contraction of 'está bom' – used constantly to mean 'okay/alright.' Also: 'tá' for 'está,' 'tô' for 'estou.'
'E aí' is a very casual greeting, like 'hey' or 'what's up.' Often followed by 'tudo bem?' or 'tudo certo?'
Brazilian Portuguese has many informal expressions – 'tudo bem,' 'beleza,' 'valeu' – that don't translate literally.
'Nossa' (short for 'Nossa Senhora' = Our Lady) is the most common exclamation in Brazil. Used for surprise, shock, or emphasis.
Adjectives must agree with the noun in gender: alto/alta, magro/magra. Masculine -o becomes feminine -a.

target: Beleza, a gente se vê amanhã.
tip: 'Beleza' means 'beauty' but is used as 'okay/cool/deal.' 'Beleza?' can also be a greeting: 'E aí, beleza?' = Hey, what's up?
'Tudo bem' is the most common greeting in Brazil. You can answer with 'tudo bem,' 'tudo ótimo,' or just 'tudo.'
'Imagina' is how Brazilians casually say 'don't mention it' or 'no worries.' Used when someone thanks you or apologizes.
'Fazer besteira' means to mess up or make a mistake. 'Besteira' can also mean something silly or nonsense.
Regular -ar past: gostar → gostaram (vocês). Third person plural: drop -ar, add -aram.
The preterite of 'ter' (to have): tive, tiveste, teve, tivemos, tiveram – completely irregular but extremely frequent.
'Bastante' = quite/very. Unlike 'muito,' 'bastante' does not change form: always 'bastante exigente.'
'Fofo/fofa' means cute and cuddly. Brazilians use it for babies, animals, and anything adorable.
'Demais' after an adjective means 'too much': 'complicada demais' = too complicated. It's very common in Brazilian Portuguese.
'Ficar' + adjective means 'to become': ficar vermelho (turn red), ficar triste (become sad), ficar bravo (get angry).
'Na correria' means in a rush/hustle. It captures the hectic pace of Brazilian city life. Very common in São Paulo.

target: Ele é um cara muito simpático.
tip: 'Simpático' = friendly/nice. In Brazilian Portuguese, this is a very common compliment. Agrees with masculine 'cara.'

target: Ela é muito inteligente e dedicada.
tip: Two adjectives with 'e' (and): both must agree with the subject. 'Inteligente' is the same for both genders.

target: Ela é morena de cabelos cacheados.
tip: In Brazil, 'morena' is a broad term that can mean brunette, olive-skinned, or dark-haired. It's used much more widely than in other Portuguese-speaking countries.

target: Tô a fim de comer pizza.
english: I'm in the mood for pizza.
tip: 'Estar a fim de' means 'to feel like' or 'to be in the mood for.' Casual but very common in everyday Brazilian speech.

english: Look at that, what a coincidence!
tip: 'Olha só' is a very common conversation opener meaning 'look' or 'check this out.' Used to draw attention to something.
'Tô de boa' means 'I'm fine/relaxed/chill.' Very informal but used constantly among friends.

english: Did you let the boss know?
tip: The 3rd person preterite is the form you'll hear most: 'ele falou' (he spoke), 'ela comeu' (she ate), 'ele partiu' (he left).

english: You're welcome, it was a pleasure.
tip: 'Ir' and 'ser' share the same preterite forms: fui, foi, fomos, foram – context tells you which verb it is.
